story.title: Guinea-Bissau Holds Referendum to Enhance Presidential Powers Amid Controversy
story.summary: Voters in Guinea-Bissau participated in a referendum to amend the constitution, aiming to increase presidential powers. The military government, which took control last year, is proposing changes that would allow the president to appoint and dismiss the prime minister. This vote precedes planned elections in December to restore civilian rule.

explore_lenses.label: What would the new constitution change?
explore_lenses.title: A shift from parliamentary power-sharing
explore_lenses.summary: The proposal would replace the parliamentary system with a more presidential one, moving key authority over the government and legislature to the head of state.

claims.text: The president would be able to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet members, rather than relying on a prime minister drawn from the parliamentary majority.
The proposed text would authorize the president to dissolve parliament and would reduce the legislature from 102 seats to 65.

The Africa Center for Strategic Studies says the accompanying reduction in electoral districts—from 29 to 12—could concentrate representation and limit smaller parties' local presence; that is an analytical assessment, not an announced legal outcome.

points: The president would be able to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet members, rather than relying on a prime minister drawn from the parliamentary majority.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The reporting describes the proposal, but the full official constitutional text and its implementation rules were not independently available in the consulted sources.
explore_lenses.note: Researched context; forecasts and viewpoints are labeled and attributed.

explore_lenses.label: Why are opposition groups boycotting it?
explore_lenses.title: Critics challenge both process and legitimacy
explore_lenses.summary: Opposition parties and civil-society figures object not only to stronger presidential powers, but also to a referendum designed under military rule and conducted amid reported limits on dissenting campaigning.

claims.text: Bubacar Turé, head of the Guinea-Bissau Human Rights League, said political parties, civil-society organizations, and traditional and religious leaders were not consulted, and said advocates of a “no” vote were not authorized to campaign.
Muniro Conté of the PAIGC argued that the proposal would weaken the prime minister and government, subordinate parliament and parties, and heighten risks of political and social tension.

The military authorities argue that a 65-seat parliament would make deliberations easier and more substantive, and that clearer presidential supremacy over the prime minister would reduce institutional instability.

The African Union Commission condemned the November 26, 2025 military takeover as an unconstitutional change of government, providing broader context for objections to a constitutional process run by the transition authorities.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the referendum?
explore_lenses.title: Results first, then a December election
explore_lenses.summary: The vote is intended to precede a planned return to elected civilian institutions, but the immediate outcome and the referendum's practical legal effect were unresolved while polls were open.

claims.text: Polling was scheduled to close at 17:00 GMT on August 30, with first provisional referendum results expected Tuesday, September 1.
Reporting before the vote identified December 6, 2026 as the planned presidential election date intended to end the transition.
General Horta N'Tam was appointed transitional president under a temporary constitutional charter that, according to Euronews, bars him from standing in the elections.
A representative of the Madem G15 party told Le Monde that a “yes” result was the most likely outcome, citing the opposition boycott; this was a forecast, not a reported result.

story_report.summary: Guinea-Bissau held a referendum on August 30 to amend its constitution, with transition authorities seeking to expand presidential authority before planned elections in December. The proposal would allow the president to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet members, shifting authority away from a government tied to the parliamentary majority. Polls were due to close at 17:00 GMT, with provisional results expected September 1; the outcome could shape the institutional rules for the planned return to civilian rule.

sections.heading: Constitutional changes reshape executive power
sections.body: The proposed constitution would also authorize the president to dissolve parliament and reduce the legislature from 102 seats to 65. The accompanying reduction of electoral districts from 29 to 12 could concentrate representation and limit smaller parties’ local presence, according to an Africa Center for Strategic Studies assessment. Military authorities say the smaller parliament would make deliberations easier and more substantive, while clearer presidential supremacy over the prime minister would reduce institutional instability.

sections.heading: Opposition challenges referendum legitimacy
sections.body: Bubacar Turé, who heads the Guinea-Bissau Human Rights League, said political parties, civil-society groups, and traditional and religious leaders were not consulted, and that supporters of a “no” vote were not authorized to campaign. Muniro Conté of the PAIGC said the proposal would weaken the prime minister and government, subordinate parliament and political parties, and increase the risk of political and social tension. The African Union Commission had condemned the November 26, 2025 military takeover as an unconstitutional change of government.

sections.heading: December transition election remains planned
sections.body: Reporting before the referendum identified December 6, 2026 as the intended date for a presidential election to end the transition. General Horta N'Tam, appointed transitional president under a temporary constitutional charter, is barred from standing in the election, according to reporting cited in the evidence. A Madem G15 representative told Le Monde that a “yes” vote was most likely because of the opposition boycott, but this was a forecast rather than a result.

unresolved.text: Final referendum results, turnout, acceptance of the result, and whether the December election proceeds as scheduled were unresolved while voting was underway on August 30.
The consulted reporting did not provide the full official constitutional text or implementation rules, nor an independent, comprehensive audit of nationwide voting conditions.

related_stories.title: Iceland Votes to Reject EU Membership Talks in Referendum
related_stories.summary: In a recent referendum, Icelanders voted against reopening talks for European Union membership, with 52.8% of voters rejecting the proposal. The decision halts the government's efforts to revive accession discussions, emphasizing concerns over the protection of Iceland's fishing waters. The outcome reflects a divided public opinion on the issue.

related_stories.summary: Norway is in mourning following the death of King Harald V at the age of 89. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, along with officials and citizens, gathered to pay tribute outside the Royal Palace in Oslo. Crown Prince Haakon is set to become the new king.

related_stories.title: Former Teleprompter Operator Fined $172,000 for Betting on Trump Speeches
related_stories.summary: Gabriel Perez, a former White House teleprompter operator, has been ordered to pay $172,000 after being found to have used insider knowledge of President Trump's speeches to place bets on the Kalshi prediction market. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) reported that he made over $100,000 from these activities.

related_stories.title: Canada Responds to Trump's Proposal to Rename Lake Ontario
related_stories.summary: In response to President Trump's suggestion to rename Lake Ontario as 'Lake America,' Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large billboard stating, 'Lake Ontario — Now and Always.' This move emphasizes Canada's stance on the matter, especially as Google has announced it will adopt the new name for U.S. users.
